narrative:
Short impact summary

The Handbook of Open, Distance and Digital Education is already functioning as a reference point in its field. Published in 2023 as an open-access handbook from Springer Nature, it has accumulated 147 citations in OpenAlex, with uptake spanning education research, technology-enhanced learning, and related policy-oriented work. A small but visible layer of online discussion includes one Bluesky mention, and the topic alignment with Quality Education suggests clear relevance to educational practice and access.

Full narrative

This handbook, authored by Olaf Zawacki-Richter and Insung Jung, was designed as a “one-stop-shop” for researchers in open, distance and digital education, and the citation record indicates that it has quickly become a synthesis point for that literature. The citing work pattern shows broad and sustained use across 2023–2026, with especially strong activity in 2024 and 2025. Most citations appear in journal articles, but the book is also being taken up in book chapters, conference papers, reviews, and editorial material, which is consistent with a work that is being used to frame both empirical studies and conceptual discussion.

The subject areas represented in the citing record point to a wide interdisciplinary footprint. Citations cluster around online and blended learning, online learning analytics, technology-enhanced education studies, digital literacy in education, and innovative teaching and learning methods. That pattern suggests the handbook is not only cited as background reading, but as a source for organizing research questions and terminology in fast-moving areas such as digital pedagogy, blended provision, and educational technology. Recent citing works also show the handbook being drawn into discussions that extend beyond higher education, including virtual laboratories, AI-integrated classrooms, micro-credentials, and digital education systems.

Geographically, the citing literature is international, with visible uptake in the United States, China, Germany, the United Kingdom, Turkey, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Spain, alongside many additional countries. The sector profile is overwhelmingly educational, which is appropriate for a handbook in this area, but the record also shows some limited reach into healthcare, government, nonprofit, and company settings. Institutional reuse is distributed rather than concentrated, although the University of South Africa, Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, and Taylor's University appear among the more frequent citing institutions.

The work’s open-access status likely supports this reach: the record identifies it as gold open access, and repository metadata shows an openly accessible instance. Adoption evidence is modest but present, with two Open Library holdings and a WorldCat record indicating library visibility. Public attention beyond formal citation is still limited in the available record, with one Bluesky mention and no event archive data, so the strongest story remains scholarly uptake rather than wider media or event-based circulation. Overall, the handbook appears to have established itself as a compact, citable synthesis in open, distance and digital education, with impact that is both intellectually central and aligned with the field’s educational mission.
